title: What goes into our decisions about competing venues

content.job: Tell the full review story in a standalone email, then connect the judgment to guided support. Do not imply that the reviewed account belonged to an Accelerator member.
content.body:
Carmen, our Google Ads lead, had explained that her starting position was to leave competitor terms in. The client's team then gave her a reason that fit this particular venue: couples were actually making that comparison.

Later in the same review, another venue came up. The team member placed it in a different market and didn't see those couples considering their venue. Carmen agreed that one should be excluded.

Both were other venues, and they called for different recommendations. What separated them was what the client's team knew about their market, considered alongside the searches Carmen was reviewing.

**A competing venue showing up in your Google Ads doesn't tell us whether its couples would also consider yours.**

Your team hears about those alternatives directly, in your conversations with couples. That's exactly the kind of information we want in front of us before we recommend keeping or excluding a competitor search.

We bring the advertising expertise and take responsibility for the recommendation. You and your team bring what you know about your venue, your market and the couples who weigh you against other venues. Good guidance needs both in the same conversation.

If you'd like to keep running your own Google Ads with that kind of support, that's what our Google Search Accelerator is built for: we build and launch your campaigns, and you run them with our experts beside you. What you know about your venue stays part of the conversation.
content.ending:
If there's a Google Ads decision you'd like expert support with, reply to this email and tell me a bit about what you're trying to solve.

Talk soon,
Whitney

caption.body:
You run your own Google Ads, and you know your market well. When other venues' names start showing up in your search terms, the right call isn't always obvious. Is that a couple who might weigh your venue too, or someone looking in a different market altogether?

In a recent review, Carmen, our Google Ads lead, went through those searches with someone on a client's team and heard two very different explanations. Couples who explored the client's venue had also considered one of the venues. The second, the team said, belonged to a market that didn't overlap with theirs, and Carmen agreed with excluding it.

That's why we don't judge another venue's relevance from its name alone. The search report starts the conversation, and your team can explain the comparison it leaves out.

When that knowledge is part of the recommendation, you get guidance that fits your venue and the couples you serve, from experts who still take responsibility for the advertising call.

content.title: Two venue names, one review
content.script:
During a venue's Google Ads review, the client's team explained why a competing venue's name made sense there.

Carmen, our Google Ads lead, was looking through the searches with someone from the venue's team. And when a bigger venue came up, that team member explained that some couples who had looked at that venue had come to them instead.

So there was a reason to give that search some consideration. Those couples could be looking at both venues.

Then they discussed another venue. The client's team explained that it was in a different market and wasn't somewhere they saw their couples making that same comparison. Carmen agreed with excluding it.

That's what matters to us in a review like this. We bring the advertising expertise, and the client's team brings knowledge of the conversations they're having with couples.

We need both before making that call. A venue name can tell us what someone searched for, but it doesn't explain whether our client's venue is a realistic alternative for them.

We want our recommendation to reflect that distinction, rather than treating every competing venue as the same decision.

caption.body:
When you run your venue's Google Ads, you want expert input that takes the account seriously and understands the market around it. Your team may hear about alternatives couples considered that wouldn't be obvious from a venue name alone.

That context came into a review led by Carmen, our Google Ads lead. A member of the client's team explained that some couples who had looked at a bigger venue had come to them instead. Later in the discussion, they identified another venue as serving a different market, without the same overlap. Carmen agreed with the recommendation to exclude that one.

The useful distinction came from combining the searches with what the client's team knew. We weren't treating every other venue as an interchangeable competitor, and the local explanation had a place in Carmen's judgment.

That's the kind of expert support we believe venue owners should have: someone who can make an advertising recommendation while understanding why a particular comparison does, or doesn't, make sense for their couples.
caption.hook: Your team's conversations with couples belong in the advertising discussion.
caption.ending: If your team hears these comparisons too, we'd want that knowledge in the conversation about your ads.

content.title: A venue name isn't the whole answer
content.script:
Should another venue's name in your Google Ads searches automatically get excluded? Honestly, I don't think a venue name can answer that on its own.

Here's how we think about it. A search report tells us what someone typed into Google. It doesn't tell us whether that couple would ever consider your venue too. And the people who often know that are you and your team, because you hear which other venues couples considered.

We saw this in a recent review. Carmen, our Google Ads lead, was going through the searches with someone on a client's team. One bigger venue was worth keeping in mind, because some of the couples who'd looked there had ended up with them. Another one, the team said, was a different market entirely, and Carmen agreed it made sense to exclude.

Two venue names in the same report, two different calls.

So when we make a recommendation about competing venues, we want both pieces in the room: the account data, and what you know about the couples who actually compare you. We still own the advertising call. We just think it's a better call when your local knowledge is part of it.

caption.body:
If you run Google Ads for your venue, you've probably seen other venues' names show up in your search terms. Some feel like obvious competitors. Some you've never heard of. And it's natural to want one simple rule for all of them.

We don't think one rule fits. In a recent review, Carmen, our Google Ads lead, heard two very different explanations from a client's team about two venues. One was a bigger venue their couples had sometimes looked at first. The other served a different market, and Carmen agreed excluding it made sense.

The account surfaced both names. Only the client's team could explain how each one related to the couples they talk with.

That's the kind of judgment we want to bring to the accounts we work on: our advertising expertise, informed by what you know about the couples who weigh your venue against others. You stay the expert on your market, and we stay responsible for the recommendation.
caption.hook: A search report can show who's looking at another venue. It can't show who'd also look at yours.
caption.ending: Your team's knowledge of who couples compare you with is worth having in every advertising conversation.

changes.after:
Should another venue's name in your Google Ads searches automatically get excluded? Honestly, I don't think a venue name can answer that on its own.

Here's how we think about it. A search report tells us what someone typed into Google. It doesn't tell us whether that couple would ever consider your venue too. And the people who often know that are you and your team, because you hear which other venues couples considered.

We saw this in a recent review. Carmen, our Google Ads lead, was going through the searches with someone on a client's team. One bigger venue was worth keeping in mind, because some of the couples who'd looked there had ended up with them. Another one, the team said, was a different market entirely, and Carmen agreed it made sense to exclude.

Two venue names in the same report, two different calls.

So when we make a recommendation about competing venues, we want both pieces in the room: the account data, and what you know about the couples who actually compare you. We still own the advertising call. We just think it's a better call when your local knowledge is part of it.

caption.body:
You know your venue's place in the local market. You also hear which other places couples explored, and those conversations can add meaning to the searches appearing in your advertising account.

In one review, our Google Ads lead, Carmen, heard from the client's team that some couples who had looked at a bigger venue had come to them instead. That information gave the competing venue search a context worth taking into account. When a separate venue came up, the team explained that it belonged to another market and wasn't a comparable option for their couples. Carmen supported excluding it.

Our view of those searches needed to reflect the difference. The account brought the names into the discussion; the client's team explained the relationship between those places and their couples.

We bring expertise to the recommendation without assuming that a report contains everything there is to know about a venue's market. Expert guidance should give relevant local knowledge a meaningful place in the decision.
caption.hook: A venue can be different from yours and still be part of a couple's shortlist.
caption.ending: That's how we want to work with venue teams: understanding the comparison before recommending what to rule out.
